To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) not clipping the perturbed sample around the clean sample is critical to prevent catastrophic overfitting for larger perturbational radii, and that (2) a stronger noise is effective in avoiding catastrophic overfitting.

(i) not clipping the perturbations around the clean sample leads to a more effective single-step adversarially trained model; (ii) using a stronger noise prior to the FGSM attack also helps in avoiding CO; and (iii) the combination of these two techniques, called Noise-FGMS, leads to the best single-step adversarial model, with a 3x faster training time than GradAlign, while achieving similar or better accuracy on a suite of benchmarks.
(1) noise and clipping are both necessary to prevent CO and (2) a single-step attack on noisy samples is sufficient to prevent CO.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the random noise in RS-FGSM is only used to reduce the magnitude of the attack, while the random step is only used to avoid CO.
the random noise is a crucial component of adversarial training, but it should not be added after the attack.
the random step in RS-FGSM is indeed necessary for preventing CO for large perturbations, but it is not the random step itself, but the fact that the random step is not clipped that prevents CO.

N-FGSEM is a simple, effective, and fast method for adversarial training.
we propose a novel single-step adversarial attack that is able to match the performance of the state-of-the-art multi-step adversarial training, while being 3x times faster.
we propose a fast and effective single step adversarial training method that is robust to large perturbations.

the random step in RS-FGSM does not contribute to the success of the method, but the addition of a random noise prior to adversarial training.
a simple and effective way to prevent CO is to avoid clipping and use a strong noise.
a careful combination of noise and clipping is crucial for single-step adversarial robustness.
